Name: graded_epistemic_strength
Title: Believe, Suspect, Know: Probing Whether LLMs Encode a Graded Epistemic-Strength Axis Distinct from Truth
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's belief about a specific item carries not only a binary truth-value but a *graded epistemic strength* (suspect < think < believe < know < certain). We hypothesize that (a) this modal-strength gradient is encoded along a recoverable, roughly monotone internal direction that is partially orthogonal to the truth direction, (b) belief-vs-knowledge confusion arises when this strength axis is miscalibrated against the model's actual answer confidence, and (c) the strength direction is causally steerable to make the model hedge or assert without changing its underlying truth judgment, and steering it toward calibrated strength improves selective-prediction reliability.
Related Work: Suzgun et al. ('Belief in the Machine'/KaBLE) and the referenced 'Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact' show behavioral conflation but treat belief as a binary truth-value, ignoring the graded modal strength ('know' vs 'suspect'). Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark; Savcisens & Eliassi-Rad 'Trilemma of Truth'; Schouten et al.) recovers static binary veracity axes. Calibration/uncertainty work (verbalized confidence, semantic entropy, P(True)) studies numeric confidence but not whether the model has an internal *lexical epistemic-strength* representation aligned to belief verbs, nor whether this axis is separable from truth and causally steerable. My prior proposals covered agent-attribution, update inertia, item-truth binding, temporal indexing, and source provenance; none address the graded modal-strength dimension of belief. This recasts belief-vs-knowledge confusion as a miscalibrated epistemic-strength encoding problem—a new lens.
Abstract: Natural language marks belief with graded epistemic strength: to 'suspect' is weaker than to 'believe,' which is weaker than to 'know.' Existing work shows LLMs conflate belief, knowledge, and fact, but treats an LLM's belief about an item as a binary truth-value with no strength dimension. We ask whether LLMs internally encode a graded epistemic-strength axis, whether it is separate from the truth direction, and whether belief-vs-knowledge confusion is a miscalibration of this axis against the model's real answer confidence. Using controlled propositions spanning a difficulty/knowability gradient (well-known, obscure, unknowable, false) paired with epistemic-modal query framings, we elicit the model's chosen belief verb and answer, and probe residual-stream activations across several open-weight models. We train ordinal probes to recover a monotone epistemic-strength score and show it is decodable along a direction partially orthogonal to the binary truth direction. We find that belief-vs-knowledge errors (asserting 'I know' for facts the model actually gets wrong, or hedging on facts it reliably answers) coincide with a mismatch between decoded strength and empirical accuracy. We then causally steer along the strength direction, flipping the model between hedged and assertive framings without altering its truth judgment, and show that steering toward calibrated strength improves selective-prediction (risk-coverage) reliability while preserving factual QA. This reframes belief-vs-knowledge confusion as a graded, tunable epistemic-strength encoding problem, with a cheap, interpretable intervention. All experiments run on <=9B open-weight models.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Assemble propositions along a knowability gradient: (i) WELL-KNOWN true facts the model reliably answers, (ii) OBSCURE true facts with medium accuracy, (iii) UNKNOWABLE/underspecified items (no ground truth answerable), (iv) FALSE claims. Draw from TriviaQA/PopQA/MMLU (with per-item empirical accuracy estimated via repeated sampling) plus fictional/underspecified templates. For each item, elicit belief via graded-modal queries ('How would you complete: I ___ that P is true? [suspect/think/believe/know/am certain]') and record the chosen verb and the model's actual answer. ~3k items with paraphrase/order randomization and controls. 2) Behavioral strength–accuracy analysis: Map chosen epistemic verb to an ordinal strength score; measure calibration = correlation between stated strength and empirical accuracy per bin. Define an epistemic-overconfidence rate (says 'know' but wrong) and over-hedge rate (says 'suspect' but reliably correct). Compare first- vs third-person framings. Models: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, plus a base-vs-chat pair. 3) Internal geometry: Extract residual-stream activations at query positions; train (a) an ordinal/linear probe for epistemic-strength and (b) a binary truth probe. Report per-layer probe accuracy, monotonicity of the strength probe across the five verbs, and subspace separation (principal angles/cosine) between the strength and truth directions. 4) Error-geometry link: Test whether decoded internal strength predicts empirical accuracy better than the model's verbalized verb (AUC/ECE), and whether strength–truth entanglement correlates with belief-vs-knowledge errors. 5) Causal steering: Recover a 'strength' direction via difference-of-means / ordinal-regression weights between low- and high-strength activations; add/subtract it and measure (i) controllability—does it shift the chosen verb along the gradient?—and (ii) specificity—does the truth judgment / answer content stay fixed? 6) Calibration fix: Steer (or a light LoRA with an auxiliary loss aligning decoded strength to empirical accuracy) toward calibrated strength; evaluate selective-prediction risk-coverage (AURC), ECE, over/under-confidence rates, and factual QA retention (MMLU/TriviaQA subset). Metrics: strength–accuracy correlation, ECE/AURC, probe accuracy & monotonicity, strength-vs-truth separation, prediction AUC, steering controllability & specificity, retained accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The chosen belief verb may be a surface stylistic choice rather than reflecting internal strength; mitigated by pairing verb choice with the ordinal probe and empirical accuracy. 2) The strength axis may entangle with truth or with topic difficulty; mitigated by controlling difficulty bins and reporting principal-angle separation. 3) Ordinal linear probes may miss nonlinear encoding; we also try MLP/ordinal-regression probes and report negatives as informative. 4) Empirical accuracy estimates require repeated sampling and may be noisy for obscure items; we bin and report confidence intervals. 5) Steering may have off-target effects on answers; specificity/retention metrics quantify this. 6) Effects may vary across model families and scale; we report per-condition rather than universal claims.
